title: Letters on hearts (2 Corinthians 3:1–6)
hook: you are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit
tomorrow: why would a tentmaker call the human body a tent?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: a sweet savor, a scent carried with sincerity. Today Paul trades the nose for the eyes: a letter anyone can read.
screen: `A SWEET SAVOR.` → `A LETTER ANYONE CAN READ.`

segments.voice: First job application, and there's the box: references. Someone has to vouch for you. In Corinth, some visiting teachers seem to have arrived with letters like that. Paul doesn't carry one. So he asks, a little dryly, "need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you?" Then he points at the people reading: "Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men."
screen: `THE REFERENCES BOX.` → `EPISTLES OF COMMENDATION?` → `YE ARE OUR EPISTLE.`

segments.voice: Anyone in Corinth can read that letter without opening a thing: just watch how these people live. And the author isn't Paul. They are "the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart." Tables means tablets. That picture belongs to Israel's prophets first: Jeremiah hears God promise, "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts." Then Paul's hardest line: "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." Christians have argued over it, and two readings stand out. One, heard in Origen and others after him: the letter is the surface sense of scripture, the spirit its deeper meaning, and reading only the surface misses the life. Its best case: Paul is talking about what's written and how it's read. The other is Augustine's: it isn't surface against depth. A command known by heart, without grace to keep it, can only condemn; the Spirit gives the life to live it. Its best case: Paul sets ink and stone against the Spirit writing on hearts, not plain meaning against hidden meaning. Neither reading makes the law the problem; Jeremiah's promise is the law written on hearts. And both keep Paul's point: the letter he cares about most is a life.
screen: `NOT WITH INK, BUT WITH THE SPIRIT.` · `WRITTEN IN THEIR HEARTS: JEREMIAH.` · `ORIGEN: SURFACE AND DEPTH.` · `AUGUSTINE: COMMAND AND GRACE.` · then, large: `A LIVING LETTER.`

segments.voice: Write one line by hand, on paper if you can: something you'd hope a person reading your life this week would find there. Look at your handwriting for a moment, uneven and entirely yours. Then fold it, and set it where you'll see it.
Letters on hearts. Paul's picture of a church as a letter from Christ, written by the Spirit, read in how people live.
Your line: a living letter, written by the Spirit and read by everyone who knows you. Rest well.

fork.reveal: the Augustine reading leans on 3:3: not with ink, not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart. the Origen reading leans on how scripture is read. both keep Paul's point: a life is the letter.

notes: Debate shape: two Christian readings of 'the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life' (3:6) are each given their best case without ranking: Origen's (letter as the surface sense of scripture, spirit as its deeper sense) and Augustine's (in De spiritu et littera: the command without grace condemns; the Spirit gives life). A scholar should confirm both summaries.

The heart-writing image is credited to Israel's prophets (Jeremiah 31:33, quoted from the KJV; Ezekiel 36:26 and the stone tablets of Exodus 31:18 in sources), and the lesson says neither reading makes the law the problem, so the law and Jewish practice are not set up as a foil. A Keeper should check the framing is fair.
'Some visiting teachers seem to have arrived with letters' is drawn from 'as some others' in 3:1 and hedged; confirm. 3:5 ('our sufficiency is of God') is left out for length.
